extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/olympiad students and beginning graduate students learning algebraic geometry and set theory
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, fundamental theorems, and worked examples about morphisms of locally ringed spaces, affine schemes, and related algebraic-geometry constructions, followed by an interlude on transfinite induction, Zorn's lemma, and basic set-theory facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphism of locally ringed spaces (Definition 87.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism of locally ringed spaces is a morphism of ringed spaces π : X → Y with the following additional property: whenever π(p) = q, the map at the stalks also induces a well-defined ring homomorphism π♯_p : κ(q) → κ(p). So we require π♯_p induces a field homomorphism on the residue fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular, since π♯(0) = 0, this implies a germ vanishes at q iff the corresponding germ vanishes at p. Intuition: the notion of 'value at a point' should be preserved. See Exercise 87.3.2 for an equivalent formulation in terms of maximal ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent local-ring condition for morphisms (Exercise 87.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The condition in Definition 87.3.1 is equivalent to requiring (π♯)img(m_Y,q) ⊆ m_X,p, i.e. a germ at q has value zero iff the corresponding germ at p has value zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes this formulation hides geometric intuition but is algebraically equivalent. This equivalence is called the 'local ring homomorphism' condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheme (Definition 87.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme is a locally ringed space for which every point has an open neighborhood isomorphic to an affine scheme. A morphism of schemes is just a morphism of locally ringed spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate example: Spec A is a scheme (take the whole space as the affine neighborhood). This is the central object; later examples and constructions exploit that locally schemes look like affine schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps between affine schemes correspond to ring homomorphisms (Proposition 87.5.1 & Theorem 87.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given π : Spec A → Spec B, the induced ring map on global sections ψ = π♯_B : B → A determines π via π(p) = ψ^{-1}(p) and on stalks π♯_p : B_q → A_p by f/g ↦ ψ(f)/ψ(g). Conversely, every ring homomorphism ψ : B → A gives a unique scheme morphism Spec A → Spec B. Thus there's a bijection between ring homomorphisms B → A and morphisms Spec A → Spec B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the 'big miracle' of affine schemes: maps of schemes compress to a single ring homomorphism. One must check continuity in the Zariski topology and that the stalk maps are local. Categorical summary: AffSch ≃ CRing^op (Corollary 87.5.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps Spec k → Spec k' correspond to field homomorphisms (Example 87.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If k and k' are fields, maps Spec k → Spec k' are in bijection with field homomorphisms k' → k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the degree-zero special case of the affine reconstruction theorem — there is nothing else to specify beyond the field map.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints for constant scheme maps via sections and stalks (Examples 87.4.4–87.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: To define a constant map X = Spec R[x] → Y = Spec R[y] sending all points to a fixed prime m ⊆ Y one must define the maps on sections so that elements vanishing off m map to units where required; e.g. a constant map to (y−3) forces y ↦ 3 in R[x], while a constant map to (y^2+1) may fail because it would require an impossible field homomorphism C = κ((y^2+1)) → κ((x)) = R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One can reason either by global sections (requirements on images of y and 1/y) or by stalk/residue-field maps; the stalk viewpoint shows existence/nonexistence via required field homomorphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic points repel smaller points (Example 87.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed (maximal) point of C[x] cannot map to the generic point (0) of C[y] because that would induce a field homomorphism C(y) → C, which does not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristic: more 'generic' points have bigger stalks and so typically cannot be targets of maps from 'less generic' points; residue-field maps often obstruct such mappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading morphisms from behavior on points (t ↦ t^2 example, Example 87.4.7 & Remark 87.4.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given how π sends points (e.g. π((x−a)) = (y−a^2) and π((0))=(0)), one can deduce π♯ on global sections: the image of y must be x^2. Equivalently, on stalks at the generic point one has C(y) → C(x) with y ↦ x^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing where germs at the generic point go often determines the whole map; more generally, behavior on closed points plus the 'value-preserving' condition fixes images of sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheme over S (Definition 87.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme over S (S-scheme) is a scheme X together with a map X → S. A morphism of S-schemes is a scheme morphism X → Y such that the diagram X → Y → S commutes. If S = Spec k, call these k-schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring an S-structure (e.g. 'over C') eliminates pathologies like nontrivial automorphisms of the base field showing up in maps (e.g. complex-conjugation automorphism of C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguished open sets are affine (Theorem 87.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a ring A and element f ∈ A, Spec A[1/f] ≅ D(f) ⊆ Spec A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary: any nonempty distinguished open subset of an affine scheme is affine; hence any nonempty open subset of a scheme is itself a scheme (Corollary 87.7.2). This is the local-affine nature of schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctured plane is not affine (Proposition 87.7.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The punctured plane U = Spec k[x,y] \ {(x,y)} is not isomorphic to any affine scheme Spec B, despite OU(U) = k[x,y]. The obstruction: in Spec B the intersection V(a)∩V(b) can contain exactly one point, leading to a contradiction with the deleted origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses global sections and the preservation-of-vanishing property for scheme morphisms; shows that having the same ring of global sections does not force an open scheme to be affine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of global sections to recover maps (construction principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a morphism π : Spec A → Spec B, the map on global sections ψ = π♯_B : B → A encodes π: π(p) = ψ^{-1}(p) and stalk maps f/g ↦ ψ(f)/ψ(g). Conversely, given ψ one constructs π and checks continuity and locality of stalk maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recipe for constructing/verifying maps between affine schemes: specify the top-level ring homomorphism and check the stated formulas and local-ring conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfinite induction and recursion (Theorem 88.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfinite induction: to prove P(β) for all ordinals β it suffices to show P(0), that P(α) ⇒ P(α+1), and that for limit λ, if P(α) holds for all α<λ then P(λ) holds. Similarly one can do transfinite recursion with zero, successor, and limit cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinals supply indices to carry out constructions beyond finite stages (ω, ω+1, ω·2, etc.). Limit stages are handled by unions (or other suitable limits) of earlier stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing a Hamel basis by transfinite recursion / union-at-limits (Section 88.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Build an increasing chain of Q-linearly independent sets S_α starting from S_0 = ∅; at successor stages add an element independent of the previous set; at limit stages take the union S_λ = ⋃_{γ<λ} S_γ. Eventually (by cardinality/Choice) one obtains a spanning independent set (a Q-basis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The union trick ensures independence carries through limit ordinals. This formalizes the intuitive 'throw in new independent numbers until spanning' argument for producing noncontinuous solutions to Cauchy's equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zorn's lemma (Theorem 88.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let P be a nonempty partially ordered set. If every chain in P has an upper bound, then P has a local maximum (maximal element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use: consider poset of independent sets ordered by inclusion; every chain has union as upper bound, so Zorn yields a maximal independent set which must be spanning. Proof sketch: climb at successor stages and use hypothesis to jump at limit stages; Axiom of Choice is used to make arbitrary chain-stage choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's diagonal argument (Lemma 89.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set X, there is no injective map ι : P(X) → X. Equivalently there cannot be a surjection X ↠ P(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs B = {x | x ∉ j(x)} to contradict surjectivity. This motivates restricting which 'collections' are sets in axiomatic set theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal language of set theory (Section 89.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set-theory statements are written using logical operators ∀, ∃, =, ⇒, ∧, ∨, ¬ and the membership relation ∈. One refers to sets indirectly by stating axioms of existence, e.g. ∃S : x ∈ S ⇐⇒ ((x=1) ∨ (x=2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundation for spelling out ZFC axioms and avoiding paradoxes like Cantor's; the chapter proceeds to define ZFC in this formal language.
